Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), a citizen of the Republic of Korea (South Korea), appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), a citizen of the Republic of Korea (South Korea), appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection. He has submitted no new evidence in support of his appeal. The Appellant asks the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to set aside the determination of the RPD and substitute a positive determination.

Pursuant to Section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. This appeal is dismissed. Background

The Appellant is a young man who has been living in Canada since 2007 as an international student. He visited South Korea in XXXX of 2014 and learned that, upon return to his country, he would be required to perform military service. He heard of problems in the South Korean military, including hazing, beatings, and deaths. He returned to Canada and thereafter made a refugee claim, fearing that he will be harmed during his military service and imprisoned if he avoids it.

The Appellant's application for refugee protection was heard on August 27, 2015. By a decision of August 31, 2015, the RPD rejected the claim. The panel concluded that there is no nexus between the Appellant's fears and a Convention ground. It found that South Korea's conscription law is one of general application, is not inherently persecutory, and that the sanctions for violating that law do not amount to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or torture. The RPD also dismissed as unproven the Appellant's claim that he will be bullied in the military because he is "Westernized" as a result of his time spent in Canada. The panel did not accept the Appellant's argument that his refusal to join the military is a form of political expression, nor did it find that the Appellant is a conscientious objector to military service. It found that the punishment for evading service-between 18 months and three years' imprisonment-is not excessive or persecutory. The RPD also concluded that, as the South Korean government is actively addressing problems in the military, and that the Appellant can avail himself of protection.

The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD made many errors in rejecting his claim, including failing to understand that torture in the military can in itself be persecutory, in failing to appreciate torture and hazing is not punishment pursuant to a law of general application, in failing to recognize that opposition to hazing and torture is related to a Convention ground, and in making a finding of state protection based on the serious efforts of the authorities, without considering whether those efforts have had practical results. ANALYSIS What is the Role of the RAD?
While the IRPA sets out grounds for appeal as well as possible remedies, it does not specify the standard by which the RAD is to review the decision of the lower tribunal.
The Appellant makes no specific submissions with respect to the standard of intervention to be applied here.

In another decision, this panel considered at some length the legislation and jurisprudence concerning the role of the RAD.1 It assessed the nature of a RAD appeal and addressed the scope and degree of deference to be shown to findings of the RPD. The panel reached the following conclusions, which it finds to also be applicable here, about the approach to be taken in a RAD appeal. The RAD's Approach

The RAD will take the following approach in considering an appeal against a decision of the RPD. It will assess all of the evidence, both that in the RPD's record and any admissible new evidence. It will consider questions of law, fact, and mixed law and fact raised by the Appellant and, where applicable, the Respondent.

Where the proceeding is a true appeal-that is, where there is no admissible new evidence-the RAD will consider the decision of the RPD, the submissions in respect of that decision, and determine whether the RPD's determination is wrong. As a true appeal is founded on the record, the RAD must conduct an independent assessment of the evidence in that record in order to determine the appeal.

Where an appeal includes admissible new evidence that speaks to an error in the RPD's decision, it is a hybrid appeal, where the RAD must consider the RPD's reasons in light of the new evidence, which may establish that the decision of the RPD is wrong.2

Where an appeal presents admissible new evidence which establishes a new, changed, or heightened risk, or otherwise changes the overall nature of the claim, this will result in a limited de novo appeal. In some such cases, the decision of the RPD may be less relevant in light of the new evidence-that is, the new evidence establishes a risk or degree of risk, or other potentially determinative matter not considered by the RPD. Unlike a true de novo proceeding, however, the RAD will not ignore the RPD's record or the findings of the lower tribunal, as these may remain relevant to the appeal.

The RAD will recognize and respect findings which the RPD was in an advantageous position to make, which will normally include credibility findings and other findings of fact. Where such deference is to be shown, the RAD will not intervene unless the RPD's reasoning process is not comprehensible or the outcome of that process is not based on and supported by the evidence.

Where the RPD's determination is entirely based on findings which warrant deference-such as an overall lack of credibility, based on oral testimony-the RAD will, having conducted its own assessment of the evidence, consider whether the RPD's reasoning process is comprehensible and whether the determination is based on and supported by the evidence.

On matters where the RPD has no advantage, the RAD will show no deference and will apply a standard of correctness, engaging in its own analysis of the evidence and reaching its own conclusion to determine if the RPD was wrong. Where the RAD finds that its conclusion does not agree with that of the RPD, the RAD will substitute its own finding and determination or, if it is unable to substitute, will refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination. The RPD's Findings

The RAD agrees with the Appellant that the RPD made several errors in determining his refugee claim. Although he did not claim to be a conscientious objector, the RPD repeatedly referred to conscientious objection as an issue, before finding that the Appellant's "personal goals do not qualify him as a true conscientious objector".3 The RPD also considered efforts made by the South Korean government to combat hazing and abuse in the military, and it concluded that "there is protection and recourse offered", without considering whether the state's efforts had any practical outcome or resulted in adequate protection. It was also wrong, as the Appellant points out on appeal, for the RPD to compare the South Korea military to others: "Sadly, there have been documented cases [of bullying] in Canada and the U.S.A. armed forces."4 The conscription-based South Korean military is not comparable to the volunteer armed forces of Canada and the U.S., even more so given that South Korea's conscripts are continually faced with the prospect of fighting against one of the largest militaries in the world.

However, these errors are not dispositive of this appeal. The RPD had no particular advantage over the RAD in assessing objective evidence about the risk faced by the Appellant, or in considering the adequacy of state protection, or whether there is nexus between his claim and a Convention ground. The RAD must conduct a full, independent assessment of the evidence in the record, and, on that basis, it is able to come to its own determination of the Appellant's refugee claim.

It is important to note here that the RPD did not make any credibility findings with respect to the Appellant. He is entitled to the presumption of truthfulness, and that presumption has not been rebutted.

The RAD finds that the key issues to be determined here are nexus, risk of harm, state protection, and whether the Appellant faces cruel and unusual punishment, or torture, if he chooses to evade military service.

Nexus: The Appellant is not opposed to military service itself, and he believes in the need to defend his country.5 He fears that he will be hazed, bullied, or tortured during his military service, and that fear of abuse makes him reluctant to join the military.

The Appellant submits on appeal that his refusal to perform compulsory military service "is a clear political opinion rejecting the state mechanism of recruiting into the military institution".6 He argues that his fear of torture and hazing amounts to an imputed opinion rejecting the state mechanism, creating a nexus to a Convention ground.

The difficulty with this argument is that the Appellant is not opposed to the state mechanism of recruitment-conscription-but rather fears illegitimate abuse that he might suffer once conscripted. The abuse he fears is not prescribed or required by the state; in fact, the government and the military have shown interest in protecting the human rights of conscripts.7 Further, the Appellant's fear is not that he will be targeted because of his anti-hazing views; rather, he fears that he will be targeted because he is a conscript.

The Appellant does fear that he will be singled out because he is "Westernized" after some years of living in Canada. He has not provided evidence, however, to establish that individuals seen as "Westernized" are targeted, and his contention therefore appears to be speculative.8

The Appellant argues that he will be jailed because of his political opinion-that is, he is opposed to hazing and torture, will therefore refuse military service, and as a consequence will be imprisoned. In the RAD's view, this does not amount to the Appellant being jailed for his opinion. If he is jailed, it will be for evading military service. If he evades military service, it is because he fears personal harm and injury. This may well be self-preservation, but it is not political opinion.

Having considered the evidence, the RAD finds that there is no nexus between the Appellant's refugee claim and a Convention ground. As such, the claim does not fall under Section 96, but must be considered under Section 97 of the IRPA.

Risk of harm: Would the Appellant's removal to South Korea subject him personally to a danger of torture, or a risk to life or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment? In assessing such risk, the question is whether "it is more likely than not that the individual would be subjected, personally, to a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if the person was returned to his country of nationality."9

The Appellant submits that there is a serious risk to all conscripts,10 that physical abuse is tolerated,11 and that suicide rates are very high in the South Korean military,12 so that he is therefore at risk.

The RAD has carefully examined the evidence in the record. It is clear that abuse of conscripts is a serious issue in South Korea; there are many examples of hazing and brutality. However, in the RAD's view, this evidence must be considered in context. Evidence presented by the Appellant to the RPD shows that, in the past five years, there have been about 3300 reported cases of assault and brutality in the South Korean armed forces.13 While this is a large number, it is an average of less than 700 cases per year in a military with over 600,000 members. To put it another way, there have been reported cases of abuse of, on average, approximately one-tenth of one percent of soldiers in recent years. The RAD is well aware of evidence that cases go unreported;14 however, even if there are ten unreported cases for each reported instance, this would increase the percentage to just over one percent.

While it is difficult to further determine the extent to which abuse takes place, one document provided by the Appellant gives anecdotal evidence that physical violence is uncommon; as a result of a "major investigation into violence in the barracks", hazing changed to punishing people with "absurdities", such as making a soldier read a book and submit a book report each day.15

The Appellant points to evidence that suicide rates in the South Korean military are much higher than in the U.S. armed forces.16 The RAD has no reason to doubt this evidence; however, it does little to establish the risk faced by the Appellant. Suicide rates in South Korea-even outside the military-are the highest in the world.17 The suicide rate in the military may be indicative of poor mental health screening and services, of a stressful environment, and of many other factors; it does not assist in assessing the risk of hazing or other abuse.

While the evidence establishes that hazing and abuse are significant problems in the South Korean military, the magnitude of that problem must also be considered in relation to the size of the armed forces. Having considered the evidence, the RAD finds it is not more likely than not that the Appellant would be subject to a danger of torture, or to a risk to life or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, upon return to South Korea.
Even if the RAD had reached the opposite conclusion, it would nevertheless reject this refugee claim on the basis of state protection.

State Protection: The RPD pointed to serious efforts made by the South Korean government to reduce abuse in the military. That analysis was incomplete; the RPD was required to consider whether those serious efforts had concrete results, leading to adequate state protection.

There have been a number of high-profile cases in South Korea in which conscripts have committed suicide or killed their fellow soldiers as a result of suffering bullying and abuse.18 In the face of public outcry, the government has pledged to address the issue. The president has called for reforms to military culture and an end to human rights abuses there; in response, the defence ministry set up a human rights council and increased the number of human rights instructors from 250 to 2000, while the National Human Rights Council launched a Military Human Rights Team.19 The government introduced a number of measures to better identify individuals who are at higher risk of "succumbing" to the harsh military environment, including an easing of the standards by which exemptions are granted for mental illness.20

The army is under close scrutiny by the government,21 and the state's efforts have had concrete results. Three hundred criminal cases were filed in the military for hazing and mistreatment of soldiers.22 After one high-profile tragedy, the army's chief of staff resigned, and the entire army suspended operations for a day-long session on human rights. Charges against soldiers alleged to have killed a conscript were upgraded from manslaughter to murder.23 Officers have been charged for not reporting abuse24 and dismissed from their posts.25 The Ministry of National Defense has improved leave, allowed more family visits, and renovated barracks to be "friendlier places".26 A new public line of communications on the issue of bullying has uncovered 4000 instances of previously unreported abuses.27

The RAD notes evidence that the South Korean justice system does not always deal appropriately with abuses in the military; there are examples of lenient sentences given to senior soldiers.28 However, the RAD has also reviewed objective evidence indicating that, of the 3300 assault and brutality cases reported since 2010, more than a thousand have resulted in punishment being administered, including fifty prison sentences, more than 350 probation sentences, about 150 suspended sentences, and more than 400 fines.29 It is not possible to ascertain from this evidence whether the punishments administered were appropriate to the offences committed; however, it is clear that the authorities do take action and administer punishment. Other evidence indicates that soldiers convicted of murdering a conscript were sentenced to as much as 45 years in prison.30

There is a presumption that South Korea, a functioning democracy, can provide adequate protection to its citizens, including those in the military. It is for the Appellant here to rebut that presumption with clear and convincing evidence. He has no personal evidence with which to rebut the presumption, and he therefore relies upon objective evidence. The RAD has carefully reviewed that evidence and finds it to be mixed. There is evidence that the South Korean authorities are aware of the problem of abuse in the military, have taken significant steps to address the issue, and that such measures have had concrete outcomes, including criminal charges and imprisonment. It is clear that the protection provided by the state here is not perfect. However, the RAD finds that the Appellant has not provided clear and convincing evidence to rebut the presumption of adequate state protection.
Even if the RAD had concluded that the Appellant faces a risk of harm upon return to South Korea, it would reject his refugee claim, and dismiss his appeal, on the basis of state protection.
Punishment: The Appellant argues on appeal that he will be imprisoned for refusing to complete his military service, and that he faces abuse in prison.31

The RAD notes that South Korea imprisons hundreds of conscientious objectors each year.32 Refusal to carry out military service is punishable by up to eighteen months in prison.33 While there is much evidence with respect to mistreatment of conscripts and with respect to the imprisonment of conscientious objectors, the Appellant has not pointed to any evidence to show that those who refuse military service face abuse or mistreatment in prison.

Prison conditions in South Korea meet international standards, and the government permits visits by independent observers.34 Prisoners can report mistreatment to the Reporting Centre for Human Rights Infringement, which investigates and can and does refer cases for correction. Food, sanitation, and medical care are adequate.35 Authorities investigate credible complaints of problematic conditions and document their investigations in a publicly-accessible manner. Prisoners have reasonable access to visitors.36

In the RAD's view, there is nothing cruel and unusual about a prison sentence of eighteen months, which is actually less than the mandatory two-year military service. The Appellant has not shown that this punishment is disproportionate or out of line with international standards.

The Appellant claims that, if he refuses to complete his military service, it will be more difficult for him to obtain employment. This assertion is supported by objective evidence.37 However, the RAD finds that such difficulty, while discriminatory, does not amount to persecution. Further, although more than 17,000 objectors to military service have been imprisoned in South Korea since 1950,38 there is no evidence that some, most, or all of these individuals were unable to find employment.
For all of these reasons, the RAD finds that the Appellant's refugee claim must fail.

The RAD acknowledges that the Appellant, in his Basis of Claim, sets out other reasons for which he wishes to remain in Canada. His mother is a victim of human trafficking and depends heavily on the Appellant and his brother. The RAD is sympathetic to this difficult situation; unfortunately, it is not a matter which this tribunal can consider, but one which is best addressed in a humanitarian and compassionate context.

Pursuant to Section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. This appeal is dismissed.
